title: Facade
summary: Offer one simple operation in front of a subsystem the caller should not orchestrate.

parts.rule: A facade presents a narrow, intention-revealing operation over a cluster of collaborating classes. Callers invoke the facade instead of wiring the subsystem steps themselves. The facade owns the orchestration order and default configuration.
parts.why: Leaky subsystems force every client to relearn a ritual of five calls. Facades reduce misuse and keep policy in one place. Overbroad facades become god objects; keep them thin.
parts.example: VideoConversionFacade.convert(inputPath, "mp4") opens the file, selects a codec, runs transcoder, writes output, and closes handles. Clients never touch CodecFactory, BitrateTuner, or TempFileManager. Home theater facade watchMovie(name) powers amplifier, starts projector, dims lights, and begins playback in order. Without the facade each UI screen reimplements that sequence and forgets to dim lights. Tests can stub the facade without spinning the whole media stack. body:
Rule. A facade presents a narrow, intention-revealing operation over a cluster of collaborating classes. Callers invoke the facade instead of wiring the subsystem steps themselves. The facade owns the orchestration order and default configuration.

Why it matters. Leaky subsystems force every client to relearn a ritual of five calls. Facades reduce misuse and keep policy in one place. Overbroad facades become god objects; keep them thin.

Worked example. VideoConversionFacade.convert(inputPath, "mp4") opens the file, selects a codec, runs transcoder, writes output, and closes handles. Clients never touch CodecFactory, BitrateTuner, or TempFileManager. Home theater facade watchMovie(name) powers amplifier, starts projector, dims lights, and begins playback in order. Without the facade each UI screen reimplements that sequence and forgets to dim lights. Tests can stub the facade without spinning the whole media stack. When to use. Use a facade when multiple clients must perform the same multi-step ritual on a subsystem. Use it at module boundaries to hide volatile internals.

When to refuse. Refuse a facade that simply renames one method with no orchestration. Refuse dumping the entire application API into one facade class. Refuse facades that prevent needed access when a client truly must customize a step — offer an escape hatch or a lower API deliberately.
